summary: Gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) is an omega-6 essential fatty acid obtained from plant seed oils such as evening primrose, borage, and blackcurrant. It is a precursor of dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid and the series-1 prostaglandins and is taken as a dietary supplement, most often for atopic eczema, premenstrual and breast symptoms (mastalgia), rheumatoid arthritis-related discomfort, and diabetic neuropathy, though the evidence is mixed and not conclusive. It is not an FDA-approved drug; it is regulated as a dietary supplement/food, and doses depend on the specific product and its GLA content. It is generally well tolerated; the main concerns are mild GI upset/headache, a theoretical lowering of the seizure threshold, and additive effects with antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs.
indications: Atopic dermatitis/eczema symptom relief (traditional/supplement use; evidence mixed)
Premenstrual syndrome and cyclical breast pain (mastalgia) (supplement use; evidence mixed)
Adjunctive support in rheumatoid arthritis-related joint discomfort
General supplementation as a source of omega-6 essential fatty acid

moa: Gamma-linolenic acid is an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid that is metabolised (largely bypassing the rate-limiting delta-6-desaturase step) to dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA). DGLA is a substrate for the synthesis of series-1 prostaglandins (e.g., PGE1) and 15-hydroxy derivatives that have anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, and it competes with arachidonic acid, potentially reducing production of pro-inflammatory series-2 eicosanoids. GLA also contributes to skin barrier lipids, which underlies its traditional use in atopic and dryness-related skin conditions.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to the source oil (e.g., evening primrose, borage) or capsule excipients
relative: Seizure disorders or concurrent drugs lowering seizure threshold (theoretical risk)
Bleeding disorders or use of anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs
monitor: Bleeding/bruising if combined with antithrombotic drugs

preg: There are insufficient safety data for GLA supplements in pregnancy, and some sources caution against use (theoretical effects on the uterus/labour with some oils). Avoid routine use in pregnancy unless advised by a healthcare professional.
lact: Data during breastfeeding are limited. GLA is a natural milk fatty acid, but supplement safety and dosing are not well established; use only under professional advice.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required; GLA is a food-grade fatty acid supplement without significant renal handling concerns at usual intakes.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required at usual supplement intakes; GLA is metabolised as a dietary fatty acid.

major: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs (warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, clopidogrel) - possible additive bleeding risk; monitor
moderate: Drugs that lower the seizure threshold / phenothiazines - theoretical increased seizure risk reported with evening primrose oil
Other supplements affecting bleeding (fish oil, vitamin E, ginkgo, garlic) - additive antiplatelet effect
minor: May modestly affect lipid/eicosanoid balance with very high intakes
interactions.food: Best taken with food; no specific food restrictions.
interactions.diagnostics: No routine laboratory monitoring required; consider bleeding-time/INR awareness if combined with antithrombotics.

counsel: This is a dietary supplement (often from evening primrose or borage oil), not a licensed medicine - tell your doctor you are taking it
Take with food and give it several weeks to see any benefit
If you take blood thinners or aspirin, mention this supplement, as it may add to bleeding risk; stop before planned surgery
If you have epilepsy or take medicines that can trigger seizures, check with your doctor first
Store away from heat and light, and do not use if the oil smells rancid
pk: Effects, if any, develop gradually over weeks of regular intake
No defined therapeutic peak; incorporated into fatty-acid pools over time
Not characterised as a drug; metabolised as a dietary fatty acid
Benefits require continued regular use; tissue fatty-acid changes persist for a time after stopping
Store soft-gels/oil in a cool, dark place away from heat and light to prevent oxidation
pearls: Not FDA-approved as a drug - GLA is a dietary supplement/essential fatty acid (commonly evening primrose, borage, or blackcurrant seed oil); guidance follows nutritional and herbal-medicine references rather than an FDA drug label
Doses are expressed as GLA content, which varies widely between oils - read the label to know the actual GLA amount
Evidence for many uses (eczema, mastalgia, neuropathy) is mixed and not definitive
Main practical cautions: additive bleeding risk with antithrombotics and a theoretical seizure-threshold concern (reported with evening primrose oil)
Allow several weeks of consistent use before judging benefit
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember, or simply skip it and continue your usual schedule - there is no need to double up. As a supplement, occasional missed doses are not harmful.
overdose: GLA has a wide margin of safety; excess intake mainly causes gastrointestinal upset (nausea, loose stools) and possibly headache. There is no specific antidote. Reduce or stop the supplement and provide supportive care; seek medical advice for large accidental ingestions, particularly in children.
